**Verdict: Revise and resubmit.** The pitch as written does not run. The full record is in `pitches/2026-11-27-teen-sadness-fell-phones-stayed/pitch.md`.

**Why the pitch fails as written**

- It repeats the argument of Jonathan Haidt's *The Anxious Generation* (2024). The publisher reports over two million copies sold (https://penguinrandomhouse.com/books/729231/the-anxious-generation-by-jonathan-haidt).
- The case against that argument is also published, for example in The New Republic (https://newrepublic.com/article/190384/cell-phones-really-destroying-kids-mental-health). I read that one as a search summary only.
- The pitch has no numbers, no named sources and no interviews done.
- The room found no source for "rewiring adolescent brains".

**The piece that can work**

Phones were blamed for the rise in teen sadness. The main CDC measure has since fallen, and the same survey shows that hourly social media use did not fall. The piece asks what changed, from inside one named school that banned phones.

The headline and the claim are my proposal, not the room's: "Teen sadness is falling. The phones are still here."

**Numbers the managing editor confirmed on the opened pages**

- Share of US high school students who reported persistent sadness or hopelessness: 28.5% in 2011 (https://www.cdc.gov/MMWR/PREVIEW/MMWRHTML/ss6104a1.htm) and 33.3% in 2025 (https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/75/su/su7501a4.htm). The 2025 figure is below the peak and above the 2011 figure.
- Students who used social media every hour or more: 37% in 2023 and 36% in 2025 (https://www.cdc.gov/yrbs/youth-health-in-focus/digital-behaviors.html).
- An Iceland study found no meaningful mental health change from school bans (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2855858).
- A US working paper found "no evidence that the school ban policy improved student mental health" (https://www.nber.org/papers/w35181).
- A study of locked phone pouches found that well-being fell in year one and was higher by year three (https://ed.stanford.edu/news/national-study-school-cell-phone-bans-shows-benefits-are-not-immediate).

**What the dissent changed**

Calder had the dissent duty. He showed that "the bans were the wrong fix" does not follow from the evidence. The fall is a national trend, and the ban studies measure single schools. I removed that claim from the shaped pitch.

He also found the combined angle on Substack (https://grimoiremanor.substack.com/p/time-trend-data-now-turning-against, snippet only). His words: "I could not find prior coverage in a general-interest magazine that puts all three together with original school reporting."

My own check agrees with him. I could not find prior coverage in a general-interest magazine that joins these three things. Three searches do not prove absence. Reporting from inside schools after a ban is also published (https://edsource.org/2026/theyre-actually-communicating-how-california-school-cellphone-bans-are-changing-classrooms/770647?amp=1, snippet only).

**What you must bring to resubmit**

1. A named school and one confirmed interview there. Without this, the piece adds nothing to what is published.
2. One claim that a reader can dispute.
3. A full read of the three ban papers.
4. A named outlet.
5. Advice that says who can act on each step and what has been measured. Wes "could not find evidence of an effect size for any parent-alone action or parent pledge."

**Still unverified**

- About 42% for 2021. Renata confirmed it through EdWeek. Nobody opened a CDC page that gives it.
- 39.7% for 2023. The 2025 CDC page says "40%".
- Calder said "from memory, unverified" that the CDC survey asks about screen time and social media. Social media is now confirmed. Screen time as a core question is not.
- Renata's claim that phone use "has probably not fallen" since 2021. One CDC measure supports it for 2023 to 2025 only.
- Most coverage links were read as search summaries only. The file lists each one.

I can extend this into a drafting brief when you want it.

# Page-one meeting: "Smartphones are rewiring our kids"

Meeting date: 2026-11-27. Source: `pitch-input.md`.

## Verdict: Revise and resubmit

The pitch as written does not run. All four editors said so in their opening takes, and none of them changed that position. The argument in the pitch is the argument of Jonathan Haidt's *The Anxious Generation* (2024), and the plan (parents, a teacher, a psychologist, a research summary, advice) can only repeat it.

A different piece is possible on the same subject. It needs reporting the pitcher has not done yet. The conditions are at the end of the next section.

## Shaped pitch

The room agreed on the question. The room did not agree on the claim. The claim below is the chair's proposal, made after the fact check, and the pitcher is free to argue for a different one.

**Angle.** Phones were blamed for the rise in teen distress. Schools and states acted on that belief. Since then, the main CDC measure of teen sadness has fallen for two survey rounds, and the same survey shows that hourly social media use did not fall. The piece asks what changed, from inside one named school that banned phones.

**Proposed claim (chair's).** Teen sadness fell, and teens did not put down their phones. A reader can dispute this. It does not say that phones are harmless, and it does not say that the bans failed.

**Working headline (chair's).** Teen sadness is falling. The phones are still here.

**Spine.**

1. A scene inside one named school in the second or third year of its phone ban. What staff and students say changed, and what did not.
2. The numbers, with the survey named. CDC Youth Risk Behavior Survey, US high school students who reported persistent sadness or hopelessness: 28.5% in 2011, about 42% in 2021, 33.3% in 2025. The 2025 figure is below the peak and above the 2011 figure.
3. The same survey on social media. Students who used social media every hour or more: 37% in 2023, 36% in 2025.
4. What three studies of school bans found. They use different designs and they do not agree.
5. What the evidence cannot show. The CDC survey asks a new sample each time, so it cannot show cause. The fall may be a recovery from the pandemic years. The dispute between Haidt and his critics stays open.
6. What a parent can do. Each step says who can take it (one parent, a group of parents, a school or district) and what has been measured for it. No step is presented as proven.

**Reader.** A parent of a child aged about 10 to 16 who has heard the case against phones and has acted on it or thinks about it. This description is the chair's; the pitcher did not name a reader.

**Proof the piece has now.**

| Claim | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|
| 28.5% of high school students reported persistent sadness or hopelessness in 2011, up from 26.1% in 2009 | Confirmed, page opened by the managing editor | https://www.cdc.gov/MMWR/PREVIEW/MMWRHTML/ss6104a1.htm |
| 33.3% in 2025 (95% CI 31.2 to 35.5) | Confirmed, page opened by the managing editor | https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/75/su/su7501a4.htm |
| Hourly-or-more social media use: 37% in 2023, 36% in 2025 | Confirmed, page opened by the managing editor | https://www.cdc.gov/yrbs/youth-health-in-focus/digital-behaviors.html |
| Iceland study, JAMA Network Open, published online 2026-10-27: schoolwide bans were not associated with meaningful changes in depressive symptoms, anxiety, hostility or well-being. 70 schools, ages 13 to 15 | Confirmed, paper opened by the managing editor | https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2855858 |
| NBER working paper w35181 (Saffer), issued May 2026 and revised November 2026: "These early results provide no evidence that the school ban policy improved student mental health." The author calls the results preliminary | Confirmed, page opened by the managing editor | https://www.nber.org/papers/w35181 |
| Stanford-linked study of locked phone pouches (NBER w35132): phone use in school fell; in year one discipline incidents rose and well-being fell; by year three well-being was higher than before | Confirmed from the Stanford Education page, opened by the managing editor. Not peer reviewed as far as that page shows | https://ed.stanford.edu/news/national-study-school-cell-phone-bans-shows-benefits-are-not-immediate |

**Conditions for the resubmission.**

1. Name the school and confirm at least one interview there. The pitcher has done no interviews and named no sources (pitcher's own account). Without this reporting the piece adds nothing to what is published.
2. State one claim that a reader can dispute. A summary of research is not enough.
3. Read the three ban papers in full. Do not describe the Iceland study as a US study. Do not mix up the two NBER papers (w35181 and w35132).
4. Remove "rewiring adolescent brains" as a stated fact, or give a source for it. The room found no source, and found a published dispute about it.
5. Replace "end with advice for parents" with section 6 of the spine.
6. Name the outlet.

## Cast

- **Renata**, novelty and saturation. Seated because this argument is among the most published on the subject.
- **Calder**, rigor and numbers. Seated because the pitch rests on a timing correlation and has no figures.
- **Imogen**, prestige and craft. Seated because the plan is a research summary plus advice.
- **Wes**, service and utility. Seated because the piece ends in advice for parents.

## Debate synthesis

**Opening takes.** All four would not run the pitch as written.

- Renata: Haidt's book makes this exact argument, including the 2012 timing and the phrase "Great Rewiring." The publisher reports over two million copies sold (https://penguinrandomhouse.com/books/729231/the-anxious-generation-by-jonathan-haidt). The objection that the evidence shows correlation and not cause is also published (https://www.npr.org/2026/01/27/nx-s1-5686531/anxious-generation-jonathan-haidt-screen-time-amazing-generation, https://www.newstatesman.com/culture/books/book-of-the-day/2024/03/how-big-tech-rewired-childhood-jonathan-haidt-anxious-generation). She did not search directly for the pitch's specific mix of interviews.
- Imogen: "phones are bad for kids" has no opponent in a general magazine, so it is a topic and not an argument. She cited the debate over the book (https://www.nbcnews.com/tech/social-media/smartphones-youth-mental-health-jonathan-haidt-book-debate-rcna145928) and a Nature review by Candice Odgers that she saw only in a secondary piece (https://www.cjr.org/the_media_today/social_media_harm_teens_jonathan_haidt.php).
- Calder: the pitch has no numbers. He found the CDC figures and saw that they fall after 2021. He could not verify "more and more schools are banning phones" or "rewiring adolescent brains."
- Wes: the advice is aimed at the wrong people. A parent cannot ban phones at a school, and a pledge only works if other families sign it.

Three editors pointed independently to 2026 evidence on school phone bans as the new ground. Calder pointed to the falling CDC numbers.

**Debate round.** Positions moved.

- Renata withdrew her own opening claim that the ban results are a new peg. She found them covered by Scientific American (https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/school-cell-phone-bans-may-boost-student-well-being-but-not-test-scores-new-study-suggests/), EdWeek (https://www.edweek.org/technology/do-student-cellphone-bans-improve-academic-achievement/2026/05), Stanford (https://ed.stanford.edu/news/national-study-school-cell-phone-bans-shows-benefits-are-not-immediate), Brookings (https://www.brookings.edu/articles/a-year-later-what-teens-tell-us-about-school-cellphone-bans/) and the University of Michigan (https://youthpolicylab.umich.edu/news/2026/school-cellphone-bans-are-mixed-and-locked-bag-study-finds). She read search summaries only. She found the CDC decline covered by the Boston Globe (https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/09/22/nation/mental-health-among-teenagers-is-improving-cdc-finds/) and EdWeek (https://www.edweek.org/leadership/teen-mental-health-is-improving-cdc-finds-then-why-are-experts-still-concerned/2026/09). She then searched for a general-interest magazine feature that argues the bans did not fix the problem: "I could not find prior coverage" in that form, and she said one search does not prove absence. Her condition: no assignment until the pitcher names a school and an interview.
- Calder withdrew his standalone "why did it fall" angle because it was already covered, and joined a combined question: phones were blamed for the rise, the rise partly reversed, and the bans show mixed results. He said the piece must not name a cause for the fall, and that a fall from the 2021 peak says little about the rise after 2012. He said "from memory, unverified" that he did not know whether the CDC survey measures phone use; Wes relayed it as "From memory, unverified, he thinks it asks about screen time and social media in recent rounds." The managing editor settled part of this (see below).
- Imogen checked the CDC figures (https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/75/su/su7501a4.htm, https://www.cdc.gov/media/releases/2024/p0806-youth-mental-health.html) and noted that CDC says the figure is still worse than ten years ago (https://www.cdc.gov/yrbs/youth-health-in-focus/mental-health.html). She accepted Calder's point about the pandemic. She held that a piece which only declines to name a cause is a survey. She would run it only as reported narrative from inside schools with one disputable claim, for example "the bans were the wrong fix for a real problem."
- Wes withdrew his own reframe. He "could not find evidence of an effect size for any parent-alone action or parent pledge." His condition: each piece of advice says who can act and what has been measured. He accepted Renata's wording for the ban studies: results are mixed and early; the strongest lasting effect is on phone use where bans are strict; mental health effects are small, delayed or absent. Renata also cited a Norwegian study said to find less bullying and fewer mental health care visits among girls (via https://www.techlicious.com/blog/school-phone-bans-teen-mental-health-study/, search summary only).

**Where the room ended.** Revise and resubmit on the combined question, with original reporting in a named school. The open disagreement is between Imogen (the writer must commit to a claim) and Calder (the claim "the bans were the wrong fix" is not supported).

## Phase 4: mandatory dissent

Assigned to Calder, because he moved furthest toward the room in the debate round.

**(a) The case that the reframe is fundamentally wrong.**

1. The claim "the bans were the wrong fix" joins two different measurements. The fall from 42% to 33.3% is a national trend. The ban studies measure single schools. Bans that reach part of the schools for a few years cannot be expected to move a national number. "Mixed" may only mean "measured too early" (https://ed.stanford.edu/news/national-study-school-cell-phone-bans-shows-benefits-are-not-immediate; snippet only for Calder, later opened by the managing editor).
2. The fall is probably a recovery from the pandemic. The one page Calder opened in full, EdWeek (https://www.edweek.org/leadership/teen-mental-health-is-improving-cdc-finds-then-why-are-experts-still-concerned/2026/09), names school mental health staffing and federal grants as possible causes, quotes John Malloy of AASA saying that without the COVID years "there wouldn't be the same level of improvement", and does not mention phones.
3. The 2011 baseline was unverified at that time. If 33.3% is above 2011, then "the crisis partly reversed" and "the crisis is still real" are both true. The managing editor later confirmed that this is the case: 28.5% in 2011.
4. Cause cannot be settled in 2,000 words. Calder cited a meta-analysis of small social media effects (https://laweconcenter.org/resources/the-forbidden-feed-adolescent-well-being-and-the-limits-of-social-media-regulation/, snippet only) against the Haidt side.

**(b) Closest existing coverage of the combined angle.** Calder searched for the combined angle and found it in pieces, all as snippets: a Substack post titled "Time Trend Data Now Turning AGAINST the 'Anxious Generation' Argument" (https://grimoiremanor.substack.com/p/time-trend-data-now-turning-against), which argues that screen use stayed high while outcomes improved; a second Substack (https://healthscaping.substack.com/p/whats-happening-in-teen-mental-health); This Week in Science (https://thisweekinsciencenews.com/blog/2026/10/22/school-cellphone-bans-youth-mental-health/); and Real Clear Investigations (https://www.realclearinvestigations.com/articles/2026/02/24/ignoring_the_science_the_curious_case_of_cell_phone_bans_1166538.html). In his words: "I could not find prior coverage in a general-interest magazine that puts all three together with original school reporting, but a search that returns blog and Substack versions of the argument means the idea is not new. Only the reporting inside named schools can be."

**Outcome.** Calder still supports a revise, but only as an open question ("what did change?"). He named the evidence that would move him to the committed claim: a 2011 CDC baseline that 33.3% has not returned to; a ban study that measures mental health for three or more years and finds no gain; and a named cause for the fall that is not phones. The first of the three is now met (28.5% in 2011). The other two are not.

The dissent changed the verdict's content. The claim "the bans were the wrong fix" is not in the shaped pitch.

## Chair's outside check

**Register.** The shaped pitch makes no claim to be first or exclusive. The headline is a statement of two survey results. The words "the phones are still here" rest on one measure (hourly social media use, 2023 and 2025) and the piece must say so.

**Saturation.** The chair ran three searches and read the search summaries only; no page was opened.

- The argument against Haidt is published in magazines and policy outlets: The New Republic, "Are Cell Phones Really Destroying Kids' Mental Health?" (https://newrepublic.com/article/190384/cell-phones-really-destroying-kids-mental-health); UnHerd, April 2026 (https://unherd.com/2026/04/the-case-against-social-media-bans/?set_edition=en); ITIF, February 2026 (https://itif.org/publications/2026/02/19/the-flawed-narrative-driving-tech-bans-for-kids/); TES (https://www.tes.com/magazine/teaching-learning/general/jonathan-haidt-anxious-generation-right-about-smartphones).
- Reporting from inside schools after a ban is also published: EdSource on California classrooms (https://edsource.org/2026/theyre-actually-communicating-how-california-school-cellphone-bans-are-changing-classrooms/770647?amp=1) and a piece on a Virginia high school (https://www.yahoo.com/news/freeing-cellphone-ban-changing-life-100038462.html). So a school scene alone is not new either.
- A search for a feature in The Atlantic, The New Yorker or The New York Times Magazine from inside a school after a ban returned no result from those three. I could not find prior coverage in a general-interest magazine that joins the falling CDC figure, the flat social media figure and reporting from a named school. Three searches do not prove absence. The pitcher must run this check again against the chosen outlet's archive.
- On "more and more schools are banning phones": a search summary of a 2025 NPR interview has Haidt saying thirty-five states have phone-free school laws or executive orders (https://www.npr.org/transcripts/nx-s1-5702348, snippet only). The NBER paper says 21 states enforced a ban in fall 2025 (https://www.nber.org/papers/w35181, opened by the managing editor). The two counts differ and measure different things.

**Chair's conclusion.** Each half of the angle is published. The combination exists on Substack. What is left for a magazine is the combination with original reporting, and the pitcher has none yet. This supports "revise and resubmit" and does not support a green light.

## Managing editor findings

Called because the room left a claim marked "from memory, unverified." The managing editor was not in the room and did not give a verdict.

1. **Does the CDC survey measure phone use?** Partly. It reports hourly-or-more social media use: 37% in 2023 and 36% in 2025, with no change and no 10-year trend (https://www.cdc.gov/yrbs/youth-health-in-focus/digital-behaviors.html, opened). This link replaces the "from memory, unverified" label for social media. Screen time appears only in a list of optional questions (https://www.upforlearning.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/YRBS-2025-Optional-Question-List.pdf, snippet only), so "screen time is in the core survey" is still unverified.
2. **2011 baseline.** 28.5%, up from 26.1% in 2009 (https://www.cdc.gov/MMWR/PREVIEW/MMWRHTML/ss6104a1.htm, opened). The 2025 figure of 33.3% is 4.8 points above it. A 2023 "poor mental health" figure that is also 28.5% is a different measure.
3. **2025 figure.** 33.3% confirmed (https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/75/su/su7501a4.htm, opened). That page says "40%" for 2023 and does not give 2021 or 2011.
4. **Teen phone use, 2021 to 2025.** No source found for the whole period. The CDC figure is flat for 2023 to 2025 only. Pew, fielded September to October 2024: 45% of teens said they spend too much time on social media, against 27% in 2023 and 36% in 2022; the share who said they had cut back rose from 39% to 44% (https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2025/07/10/10-facts-about-teens-and-social-media/, opened). This measures what teens think, not hours of use.
5. **JAMA Network Open study.** Confirmed. "School Phone Bans and Adolescent Mental Health in Iceland," published online 2026-10-27, first author Elena Bonilla Aparicio; 23,938 observations from 70 Icelandic schools; 22 schools adopted bans between 2018 and 2023 (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2855858, opened). It is Iceland only. It covers schoolwide bans; the word "daytime" came from the secondary source. The authors list limits: ban schools differed at the start, and phone use in school was not measured objectively.
6. **NBER w35181.** Confirmed, with a date correction: issued May 2026, revised November 2026. Data: National Survey of Children's Health, 2016 to 2025, about 11,500 children aged 14 to 17 per year (https://www.nber.org/papers/w35181, opened).
7. **Stanford-linked pouch study.** Findings confirmed from the Education school page, dated 2026-05-04; authors named there are Thomas Dee, Matthew Gentzkow and Hunt Allcott with researchers from Duke, Michigan and Penn; it is NBER working paper w35132 (https://ed.stanford.edu/news/national-study-school-cell-phone-bans-shows-benefits-are-not-immediate, opened). The second link the room used (https://news.stanford.edu/stories/2026/11/school-phone-bans-research) returned HTTP 403 and was not read.

## Gaps carried from intake

The pitcher said "just start," so these were not asked.

- No interviews are done and no sources are named.
- No outlet is named. No outlet guide was loaded.
- The pitch gave no news peg. The room found two: the 2025 CDC figures and the 2026 ban studies. Both are already reported as news.
- The pitcher did not say whether they know the existing coverage.
- The pitch's own claims carry no sources: the 2012 timing, "hours a day," "rewiring adolescent brains," and "more and more schools are banning phones."

## Claims still unverified after the check

- About 42% for 2021. Renata confirmed it through EdWeek (https://www.edweek.org/leadership/cdcs-latest-youth-behavior-report-offers-a-narrower-look-at-teen-health/2026/09). Nobody opened a CDC page that gives it.
- 39.7% for 2023. Calder's link is https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/73/su/su7304a9.htm, read as a search summary. The 2025 CDC page says "40%."
- Screen time as a core question in the CDC survey. Calder's "from memory, unverified" label stays on this part.
- Renata's claim that phone use "has probably not fallen" while sadness fell. Supported for 2023 to 2025 by one CDC measure. No figure found for 2021.
- The November 2026 Stanford news story (HTTP 403).
- The Odgers review in Nature and the 72-country analysis it cites. The room saw these only in secondary pieces.
- The Brookings survey, the Boston Globe pieces, the Scientific American piece, the Norwegian study, the Substack posts and every link in the chair's outside check. All were read as search summaries.
- "Over two million copies sold" for Haidt's book. Renata gave the publisher's page as the source; the record does not show that she opened it.
- The count of states with school phone bans. Two different counts, one of them from a snippet.
- "Rewiring adolescent brains." No source found.

## Verdict: Kill it, as pitched

All four editors voted to kill the pitch. The pitch repeats the argument of Jonathan Haidt's *The Anxious Generation* (2024). The dispute about that argument is also covered (https://www.nbcnews.com/tech/social-media/smartphones-youth-mental-health-jonathan-haidt-book-debate-rcna145928, https://www.cjr.org/the_media_today/social_media_harm_teens_jonathan_haidt.php). The plan of parents, a teacher, a psychologist and advice adds no new reporting. Credit to the pitcher: the pitch says no reporting is done yet.

## One narrower pitch is open: Revise and resubmit

The room would read this pitch again: one named school, in year two or three of a phone ban, tested against its own records. The condition is strict. The school must have a baseline from before the ban, the same survey each year, and it must release the data. Without that school, this pitch is also dead. The managing editor gave the narrower pitch the same verdict.

## What the dissent found

Desmond moved furthest toward the consensus, so he argued against it.

- He found the closest existing piece: Boston Globe, August 4, 2026 (https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/08/04/metro/new-hampshire-schools-cellphone-ban-results/). He called the replacement a rewrite of it. The managing editor opened the same piece and says that overstates the overlap. It is a statewide story in the first year of a ban, with no year-three data.
- One school's numbers have no comparison group. They cannot separate the ban from a new principal.
- The studies test bans during school hours only. A null result does not show that phones are harmless.
- The national pouch study shows well-being down in year one and up by year three. So the choice of school chooses the conclusion.

## My check from outside the room

- The narrow angle is partly covered. EdWeek ran a three-year story on one Kansas middle school (https://www.edweek.org/technology/cellphone-ban-adopters-share-how-they-did-it-and-how-its-changed-students/2025/05). I saw the search summary only.
- I could not find prior coverage, in a general-interest outlet, of one named school tested against the year-one and year-three pattern with its own well-being survey. Three searches do not prove the space is empty.
- The room said "the only thing I would fund". The searches do not support "only". The shaped pitch does not use that word.

## What the managing editor settled

- The pouch study is NBER w35132, issued April 2026 (https://www.nber.org/papers/w35132). It covers more than 43,000 schools (https://siepr.stanford.edu/news/school-cellphone-bans-deliver-benefits-not-right-away). The November Stanford link that Margit gave returned 403. That claim was marked "from memory, unverified", and these two links now replace the label.
- The Iceland study exists: JAMA Network Open, DOI https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.40893, nearly 24,000 students. The details come from a search summary. No one opened the JAMA page.
- Saffer's paper (https://www.nber.org/papers/w35181) supports "no clear evidence so far, results preliminary". The data window and the number of states with data from after a ban are not settled. The managing editor could not read the PDF.

## Still unverified

- The 16% rise in suspensions in year one: search summary only.
- "Roughly 4,600 schools": search summary only, meaning unknown.
- The Kansas figures (absenteeism 39% to 11%, suspensions down 70%): search summary only.
- South Australia's two-year wellbeing data: from memory, unverified.
- Any figure for teen anxiety or depression rates. The pitch gives none.

## Gaps from intake

The pitch has no named outlet, no named expert or study, and no source for the 2012 claim or the "rewiring" claim. The pitcher's access is unknown, and access decides the narrower pitch.

The full record is in `pitches/2026-11-27-one-school-phone-ban-year-three/pitch.md`. If you find the school, I can build the drafting brief from that file.

Meeting date: 2026-11-27. Source: `pitch-input.md`. Target: an unnamed general-interest magazine, about 2,000 words.

## Verdict

**Kill it**, as pitched.

The pitch repeats an argument that has been the main frame on this subject since Jonathan Haidt's *The Anxious Generation* (2024). The dispute about that argument is also covered. The plan (two or three parents, a teacher, a psychologist, a research summary, advice) adds no new reporting to it. All four editors voted to kill, and no check after the meeting changed that.

A different, narrower pitch is open: **Revise and resubmit**, on one condition. The pitcher must name one school, several years into a phone ban, that kept its own numbers from before the ban and will release them. Without that school, the narrower pitch is also dead. The managing editor gave the narrower pitch the same verdict, Revise and resubmit.

## The shaped pitch (the version the room would read again)

**Angle.** A national study says school phone bans make student well-being worse in the first year and better by the third. This piece tests that pattern in one named school, using the school's own records, and reports what the ban did not change, including the phone at home in the evening.

**Working headline.** "Year Three of the Phone Ban: What One School's Own Numbers Show". This headline is the chair's suggestion, not a room decision.

**Spine.**
1. Open in the school, in year two or three of the ban, with a principal who will say what did not work.
2. Give the school's records from before and after the ban: discipline, attendance, and a well-being survey if the school asked the same questions each year. State the denominator and the method for each number.
3. Set those records against the comparison-group studies: the national pouch study (NBER w35132), Saffer (NBER w35181) and the Iceland study in JAMA Network Open. Interview the study authors on the record.
4. Say plainly that a null result on bans during school hours does not show that phones are harmless, and does not test use at night. Hold the dispute between Haidt and his critics to two paragraphs.
5. Close with actions, each labeled by who can take it: one parent alone at home, a few families together, the school or the state. Run an action only if the school's results support it. If the results support no action at home, say so.

**Reader.** A parent or teacher whose school already has a ban, or will soon, and who has already read the argument that phones cause harm. Roughly 40 states now have school phone rules, and the count varies by tracker (https://ballotpedia.org/State_policies_on_cellphone_use_in_K-12_public_schools, https://www.pbs.org/newshour/education/a-majority-of-u-s-states-now-have-laws-banning-or-regulating-cellphones-in-schools).

**Proof.** None yet. Credit to the pitcher: the pitch says no reporting is done, and the planned sources are parents, a teacher and a child psychologist. The shaped pitch needs different sources: the school, its records, its principal, and the study authors.

## Cast

- **Margit Oyelaran**, novelty and saturation.
- **Desmond Krall**, rigor and numbers. He also did the mandatory dissent.
- **Lucia Ferrante-Bose**, prestige and craft.
- **Hank Tolliver**, service and utility.

## Debate synthesis

**Opening takes.** All four leaned kill.

- Margit: the pitch follows the sequence of Haidt's book: 2012 timing, phones in place of play, rewiring, school bans, pledges, advice. Candice Odgers answered the book in Nature in March 2024. NBC News and CJR covered the dispute (https://www.nbcnews.com/tech/social-media/smartphones-youth-mental-health-jonathan-haidt-book-debate-rcna145928, https://www.cjr.org/the_media_today/social_media_harm_teens_jonathan_haidt.php).
- Desmond: the pitch makes a causal claim from two lines that rise together and does not mention that researchers contest it. He cited Odgers' Nature review (https://internet.psych.wisc.edu/wp-content/uploads/532-Master/532-UnitPages/Unit-11/Odgers_Nature_2024.pdf), Amy Orben's "very small" associations per a secondary summary (https://cityam.com/?p=2145926), and Haidt's reply (https://www.afterbabel.com/p/social-media-debate-longitudinal). He read search summaries only. He could not verify any figure for teen anxiety or depression rates, and the pitch gives none.
- Lucia: a topic, not an idea. She added https://newrepublic.com/article/190384/cell-phones-really-destroying-kids-mental-health. Search summaries only.
- Hank: the advice ending is the thinnest part. A parent with two jobs cannot join a pledge that needs the whole class. Pledges such as "Wait Until 8th" are covered (https://le.utah.gov/interim/2026/pdf/00000281.pdf).

**Debate round.** Each editor first offered a different replacement. The round removed three of them.

- The dispute over the evidence, as the spine (Desmond's): withdrawn. Margit found explainers of that dispute from Oxford, 2025-05-13 (https://www.ox.ac.uk/news/2025-05-13-expert-comment-how-social-media-debate-teen-mental-health-missing-point), Big Think (https://bigthink.com/the-present/debate-on-social-media-and-mental-health/) and Science News (https://sciencenews.org/article/social-media-teens-mental-health). Desmond did not open those links.
- One family that took the phones away (Lucia's first version): dropped. Margit found the format at Axios (https://www.axios.com/2024/06/25/no-smartphone-teen-childhood-pledge), Good Morning America (https://www.goodmorningamerica.com/news/story/parents-empowered-wait-8th-keeping-kids-smartphone-free-49157334) and Axios Detroit on 2026-11-13 (https://www.axios.com/local/detroit/2026/11/13/metro-detroit-parents-delay-smartphones-for-kids). Lucia did not open those links.
- "What happened after the bans", at national scale (Margit's first version): conceded as no longer new. EdWeek (https://www.edweek.org/technology/do-student-cellphone-bans-improve-academic-achievement/2026/05), SIEPR (https://siepr.stanford.edu/news/school-cellphone-bans-deliver-benefits-not-right-away) and Michigan (https://fordschool.umich.edu/news/2026/lockable-phone-pouches-schools-improve-student-well-being-over-time-not-test-scores-or) already run it. Margit took those links from Hank and Lucia and did not open them.
- "What works if you cannot ban the phone" (Hank's): kept only as a labeled closing section. Hank said "I could not find prior coverage" of that angle, and he did not run a full search for it. Margit said of the evening-phone gap, "I could not find that gap covered", and she did not search for it directly.

**Where the room ended.** Kill as pitched. Green only if the pitcher names one school in year two or three of a ban, with its own before-and-after numbers and a principal who will say what did not work, by the next meeting. Lucia also cited a Harvard study reported in Fortune as one to two extra weeks of learning, not peer reviewed (https://fortune.com/2026/11/19/harvard-phone-ban-study-school-kids-learn-two-weeks), from a search summary.

## Mandatory dissent

Assigned to Desmond, because he moved furthest toward the consensus (he withdrew his own replacement and backed Margit's). His task was to argue against the room's replacement piece.

**Has it been done?** He says yes, recently.

- Closest match, opened by him: Boston Globe, August 4, 2026 (https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/08/04/metro/new-hampshire-schools-cellphone-ban-results/). It follows New Hampshire's "bell-to-bell" ban, uses Manchester High School as the local example, cites a voluntary state survey of 1,399 teachers and administrators (79% of teachers said the ban reduced distractions, 38% saw better academic outcomes), and cites the national pouch study. Its headline says "not silver bullet".
- From search results only, not opened: EdWeek (https://www.edweek.org/technology/do-school-cellphone-bans-work-what-early-findings-tell-us/2025/10), Good Morning America (https://goodmorningamerica.com/family/story/1-year-school-cellphone-bans-educators-report-calmer-133595015), UFT (https://www.uft.org/news/teaching/learning-curve/statewide-cellphone-ban-1-year-later), NZ Herald (https://nzherald.co.nz/nz/school-phone-ban-one-year-on-student-survey-reveals-mixed-feelings-about-its-success/JAH3XFN3LVDM7MLI5OMSHWXKBA).
- On the null results: ProMarket on Saffer, August 3, 2026, opened (https://www.promarket.org/2026/08/03/school-smartphone-bans-show-no-effect-on-youth-mental-health/). Marginal Revolution (https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/05/early-evidence-on-school-smartphone-bans-and-mental-health.html) and Scientific American (https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/school-cell-phone-bans-may-boost-student-well-being-but-not-test-scores-new-study-suggests/), search results only.
- He did not find a general-interest magazine feature on the null mental health results. That was one search pass.

**What would make the replacement fundamentally wrong?**

1. One school's before-and-after numbers have no comparison group. They cannot separate the ban from a new principal or a different cohort. Saffer and Iceland use comparison groups and found nothing.
2. The studies test bans during school hours. The harm in the original claim is mostly outside school hours. A headline that says bans do not work could be read as clearing phones.
3. The pouch study shows well-being down in year one and up by year three. So the choice of school chooses the conclusion.

**Where he landed.** Kill the original. The replacement as the room shaped it is close to the Boston Globe story, and he would kill that too. The one gap he found is the difference between year one and year three. Evidence that would change his mind: a school that kept its own baseline from before the ban, asked the same survey each year, and will release it.

**Effect on the verdict.** The room's condition got stricter. "A named school with numbers" became "a named school with a baseline from before the ban, the same survey each year, and a release". The shaped pitch above carries his three objections in spine items 2, 3 and 4.

## Chair's outside check

Done by the chair with three web searches, after the dissent. Search summaries only. The chair did not open the pages.

- **Is the narrow angle saturated?** Partly. A single-school, three-year story exists in the education trade press: EdWeek on a middle school in McPherson, Kansas (https://www.edweek.org/technology/cellphone-ban-adopters-share-how-they-did-it-and-how-its-changed-students/2025/05). The search summary gives chronic absenteeism falling from 39% to 11% and suspensions down 70%. Those two figures are from a search summary and are not confirmed. Brookings has teens one year later (https://www.brookings.edu/articles/a-year-later-what-teens-tell-us-about-school-cellphone-bans/); its summary says teens in strict-policy schools mostly report no effect on well-being, and that reported phone use at school went up through the 2025-2026 school year. EdWeek also covered the Harvard achievement study (https://www.edweek.org/technology/students-made-more-math-reading-progress-after-their-schools-banned-phones/2026/11).
- **What the chair did not find.** I could not find prior coverage, in a general-interest outlet, of one named school tested against the year-one and year-three pattern with its own well-being survey. Three searches do not prove the space is empty.
- **Register.** The room's words "the only thing I would fund" and "the only new material" claim more than the searches support. The shaped pitch above does not say "only", "first" or "no one has".
- **A conflict the check raised.** One search summary said the pouch study covered "roughly 4,600 schools using Yondr pouches". The editors said more than 43,000. See the managing editor's finding D.

## Managing editor findings

The chair sent the managing editor every claim that left the room marked "from memory, unverified", word for word, plus the two figure conflicts. The managing editor was not in the room. "Opened" means the managing editor read the page.

**A. Margit's claim:** "a Stanford-linked pouch study reported a first-year dip in wellbeing and a recovery by year three (https://news.stanford.edu/stories/2026/11/school-phone-bans-research)". **Mostly holds, with a wrong link.** The study is NBER w35132, "The Effects of School Phone Bans: National Evidence from Lockable Pouches" (Allcott, Baron, Dee, Duckworth, Gentzkow, Jacob), issued April 2026 and revised September 2026 (https://www.nber.org/papers/w35132, opened). Stanford's write-up is dated May 2026 (https://siepr.stanford.edu/news/school-cellphone-bans-deliver-benefits-not-right-away, opened). Well-being fell in year one and was above the baseline by year three. The news.stanford.edu November URL returned 403 and was not opened. Use the NBER or SIEPR link.

**B. The Iceland claim (marked unverified by Hank):** "a JAMA Network Open study of about 24,000 Icelandic 13- to 15-year-olds, reported as October 27, 2026, found no meaningful mental health gain from bans". **Holds, with corrections.** Bonilla Aparicio E et al., "School Phone Bans and Adolescent Mental Health in Iceland," JAMA Netw Open 2026;9(10):e2640893, DOI https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.40893. The details come from a search summary; the managing editor did not open the JAMA page. The summary gives 23,938 students aged 13 to 15, 70 schools, 22 with bans, and a difference-in-differences design. The media release is dated October 27, 2026 (https://media.jamanetwork.com/media-releases/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.40893, search result only). Write "nearly 24,000".

**C. The Saffer claim (marked unverified by Hank):** "an NBER working paper by Saffer (https://www.nber.org/papers/w35181) found no clear evidence of improved wellbeing". **Holds as worded. The detail figures are not settled.** The NBER page (opened) says 2016 to 2025, about 11,500 children aged 14 to 17 per year, and 21 states enforcing bans in fall 2025. Saffer's own ProMarket piece from August 3 (opened, https://www.promarket.org/2026/08/03/school-smartphone-bans-show-no-effect-on-youth-mental-health/) says 2016 to 2024 and "currently only three states have any post-ban data". The managing editor could not read the paper PDF. The managing editor's inference, marked as an inference: the November revision added the 2025 survey year, and "21 states" counts states with bans, not states with data from after the ban. Safe wording: "no clear evidence so far, results preliminary".

**D. The pouch study's size.** "More than 43,000 middle and high schools nationwide" is confirmed (SIEPR link above, and https://impact.stanford.edu/article/what-national-evidence-reveals-about-strict-school-phone-bans, both opened). K-12 Dive gives a third figure: phone-use data from 40,542 schools (https://www.k12dive.com/news/school-cellphone-study-academics-discipline-well-being-attendance-bullying/819236/, opened). The 4,600 figure was on no page the managing editor opened. The 16% rise in suspensions appears only in a search summary; the opened pages say suspensions rose and give no percentage.

**Novelty of the narrow pitch.** Partly covered. The managing editor opened the Boston Globe piece and reports that it is a statewide New Hampshire story with a state survey, in the first year of the ban, with no year-three data. So "a rewrite of the Globe piece" overstates the overlap. The year-one dip and year-three recovery are already reported nationally. On one named school followed over several years with its own data, in the New York Times, Atlantic, New Yorker or Washington Post, the managing editor says "I could not find prior coverage", and did not search those outlets' sites directly. Also from the managing editor, from memory, unverified: South Australia's two-year wellbeing data (https://www.education.sa.gov.au/department/media-centre/our-news/wellbeing-data-shows-positive-effects-of-mobile-phone-ban, search result only), a state system, confounded by a $50 million spending program.

**Managing editor's verdict on the narrow pitch:** Revise and resubmit.

## Gaps carried from intake

The pitcher skipped intake, so none of these is confirmed.

- No named outlet. No editor could judge fit.
- No news peg in the pitch. The room supplied one: the ban studies published from April to November 2026.
- No named study, expert, school or pledge. "Experts say" has no name attached.
- The claim that rates rose "around 2012" and the claim of "rewiring" brains have no source. Both stay out until the pitcher sources them.
- The pitcher did not say whether they know the existing coverage.
- The pitcher's access and standing are unknown. This decides the narrow pitch: it needs a school that will open its records.

## Claims still unverified after the checks

- The pouch study's 16% rise in suspensions in year one. Search summary only. Not on any opened page.
- "Roughly 4,600 schools using Yondr pouches." Search summary only. Its meaning is unknown.
- McPherson, Kansas: chronic absenteeism from 39% to 11% and suspensions down 70%. Search summary only.
- Saffer: the data window (2016 to 2024 or 2016 to 2025) and the number of states with data from after a ban (three, as of August). The paper PDF was not read.
- Iceland: the study's details come from a search summary and one secondhand article. No one opened the JAMA Network Open page.
- South Australia's two-year wellbeing data: from memory, unverified.
- Orben's "very small" associations: from a secondary summary, not the paper.
- Odgers' Nature review and every effect size in the Haidt dispute: search summaries only, not checked against the originals.
- The Harvard study's one to two extra weeks of learning: search summary of a Fortune report, not peer reviewed.
- Any figure for teen anxiety or depression rates. None was verified, and the pitch gives none.

# Page-one meeting: the second year of a school phone ban

Date: 2026-11-27. Target: an unnamed general-interest magazine, about 2,000 words (credit: the pitcher). No outlet guide applied, because the pitch names no magazine.

## Verdict: Revise and resubmit

The pitch as written ("Smartphones are rewiring our kids") is a kill. All four editors and the managing editor reached that independently. It restates the thesis of Jonathan Haidt's "The Anxious Generation" (Penguin Press, 26 March 2024: https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/729231/the-anxious-generation-by-jonathan-haidt/9780593655030), and the dispute over that thesis is already heavily covered.

The replacement angle below is worth a second submission, but it is not a green light. The finding it rests on is already reported as news, the study is a working paper, and the pitcher has no school, no access and no named sources yet (credit: the pitcher's own plan says no reporting is done). The piece only works if a named school lets the writer in and shares its own figures.

## The shaped pitch

**Angle.** One named school in its second year of a phone ban. A national study says the first year of locking phones away brings more disciplinary incidents and a suggestive drop in student wellbeing, and that things recover later. The adults at this school are in the middle of that curve and do not know whether their school will follow it. What do they do with a rule that parents overwhelmingly wanted and that the first-year numbers do not flatter?

**Working headline.** "Year Two of the Phone Ban"

**Spine.**
1. Open inside the school: a specific moment from the second year of the ban, with the principal's or a teacher's own first-year numbers.
2. How the rule got there. Bans spread on conviction: 39 US states and 106 countries, per a US News headline (https://www.usnews.com/news/national-news/articles/2026-08-10/39-u-s-states-and-106-countries-now-prohibit-phones-in-class, search snippet only), and 93% of parents favoring some restriction (https://www.brookings.edu/articles/survey-parents-and-teens-support-school-cellphone-bans/, search snippet only).
3. What the study measured and what it did not. State the design, the working-paper status and the absolute effects. State plainly that no ban study here measures teen depression or anxiety, so this piece does not settle the argument the original pitch was about.
4. The complications: test scores near zero in one study and small gains from year one in another; teens reporting that phone use at school crept back up.
5. The decision the school's adults face, and the honest statement that nobody knows whether year three arrives for this school. A national average does not predict one school.
6. Close with a short section of actions labeled by who can take them (parent alone, parents together, school, state). Each label says what has been measured for it, including "nothing found" where that is true. It is the last scene, not the verdict.

**Reader.** A parent or teacher who already supports phone limits and assumes the question is settled. The person who can act is narrower: a principal, a school board member, or a parent group in a school that has a ban or is about to adopt one.

**Proof the writer must bring back.**
- A named school that used lockable pouches (the study covers pouch schools; a school with a different kind of policy does not match the evidence), with a principal or teacher on record and the school's own discipline and survey figures for before, year one and year two.
- The paper read in full, with the year-by-year results and absolute numbers. PDF: https://web.stanford.edu/~gentzkow/research/PhoneBans.pdf (nobody in this meeting opened it).
- An author of the study and one named critic on record. No "experts say".

## What the evidence says, as far as it was checked

- **The pouch study.** "The Effects of School Phone Bans: National Evidence from Lockable Pouches", NBER Working Paper 35132, by Allcott, Baron, Dee, Duckworth, Gentzkow and Jacob, issued April 2026, revised September 2026 (https://nber.org/papers/w35132; abstract page opened by Teodor and the managing editor). Staggered difference-in-differences, not randomized, pre-registered. Phone use falls. Disciplinary incidents rise in year one and the effect later fades. There is "suggestive evidence that student well-being falls" in year one, and effects "appear to recover and become positive in later years". Test scores stay close to zero on average, with a modest gain in high school math and small negative effects in middle schools.
- **Sample and year three.** The abstract gives no sample size and does not say "year three". Stanford-affiliated pages say more than 43,000 middle and high schools over about three years, and that "in the third year, student well-being was higher than before the phones were stashed away" (https://siepr.stanford.edu/news/school-cellphone-bans-deliver-benefits-not-right-away). Scientific American says the longest-enforcing schools had "no more than three years of postadoption data" (https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/school-cell-phone-bans-may-boost-student-well-being-but-not-test-scores-new-study-suggests/). Year three is the outer edge of the data.
- **The November national study.** Reports test-score gains worth a week or two of school per year, starting in year one, not yet peer reviewed per Teodor's search summary (https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/11/17/nation/new-evidence-shows-school-phone-bans-are-gradually-improving-test-scores/, https://fortune.com/2026/11/19/harvard-phone-ban-study-school-kids-learn-two-weeks). Search summaries only.
- **Florida.** NBER working paper: no score change in year one, when suspensions spiked, then about 1.1 percentile points in year two in schools with heavy prior phone use (https://www.nber.org/digest/202512/school-cell-phone-bans-and-student-achievement). Search summary only.
- **England.** 1,227 students in 30 schools; no link between restrictive policies and wellbeing, and no drop in total phone use (https://www.birmingham.ac.uk/news/2025/school-bans-alone-not-enough-to-tackle-negative-impacts-of-phone-and-social-media-use). It is a one-time snapshot, so it describes ban schools today and cannot show that a ban failed.
- **Enforcement.** Teens report that phone use at school rose over 2025-26 despite bans, least in the strictest schools (https://www.brookings.edu/articles/a-year-later-what-teens-tell-us-about-school-cellphone-bans/).
- **Spread.** Bell-to-bell bans at 74% of schools in 2025-26, up from 60% (https://fordschool.umich.edu/news/2026/first-its-kind-national-educator-survey-reveals-both-promise-and-peril-school-cell-phone).
- **The original pitch's trend.** Persistent sadness or hopelessness among US high school girls went from 35% in 2011 to 57% in 2021, and among boys from 21% to 29% (https://www.cdc.gov/nchhstp/director-letters/cdc-releases-yrbs-summary-report-2011-2021.html). All students: 28.5% in 2011 (https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/ss6104a1.htm), about 42% in 2021 and 39.7% in 2023 (https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/73/su/su7304a9.htm). The causal link to phones is disputed: Candice Odgers in Nature (https://internet.psych.wisc.edu/wp-content/uploads/532-Master/532-UnitPages/Unit-11/Odgers_Nature_2024.pdf), Haidt's reply (https://www.afterbabel.com/p/social-media-debate-longitudinal?open=false), NBC News on the debate (https://www.nbcnews.com/tech/social-media/smartphones-youth-mental-health-jonathan-haidt-book-debate-rcna145928).

## Debate synthesis

**Opening.** All four rejected the pitch as written. Odalys and Marguerite called it Haidt's book at magazine length and listed the existing coverage of the dispute: NBC News, the Nature review, After Babel (links above), Platformer (https://platformer.news/anxious-generation-jonathan-haidt-debate-critique/), The New Republic (https://newrepublic.com/article/190384/cell-phones-really-destroying-kids-mental-health), CJR (https://www.cjr.org/the_media_today/social_media_harm_teens_jonathan_haidt.php) and Fortune (https://fortune.com/well/article/anxious-generation-researcher-social-media-youth-mental-health-crisis-criticism). Odalys read search summaries only. Teodor showed the CDC trend is mostly about girls and flattened after 2021. Dez said the advice ending serves only parents who have not yet handed over a phone. All four pointed to the same replacement: school phone bans spread faster than the evidence for them.

**Debate.** Odalys then checked that replacement and found it already reported as news: NPR (https://www.npr.org/2026/05/07/nx-s1-5810471/new-study-measures-whether-school-cell-phone-bans-actually-work), Fast Company (https://www.fastcompany.com/91643972/school-phone-bans-working-so-far-heres-early-studies-show), US News, EdWeek (https://www.edweek.org/technology/do-student-cellphone-bans-improve-academic-achievement/2026/05, https://www.edweek.org/technology/do-school-cellphone-bans-work-what-early-findings-tell-us/2025/10?view=register), the Boston Globe and Fortune (https://fortune.com/2026/05/08/phone-bans-classroom-no-effect-school-test-scores-math-reading/). All from search snippets. Marguerite dropped her first scene ("certain parents versus a study") as wire copy and moved to one school in its second year. Teodor moved from kill to revise with four conditions: state each study's design and peer-review status; give absolute effects next to relative ones; do not let a test-score result stand in for a wellbeing claim; name the experts. Dez and Marguerite agreed the closing action section stays as a short last scene. Teodor corrected Marguerite: do not write "no study shows a wellbeing gain"; say wellbeing results are mixed and unsettled. Odalys downgraded her own "worse first, better later" explanation of why the studies disagree to a hypothesis, because only about two of the four studies measure change over time.

**Where it ended.** Four votes for revise toward the one-school, second-year piece, each with a kill condition: no school access, or the paper's year-by-year numbers do not hold.

## Phase 4: mandatory dissent (Teodor Vance)

Teodor moved furthest toward the consensus, so he argued against it.

**(a) What would make the pitch wrong.**
1. The room misstated its own source. In the abstract, discipline "fades"; it does not get better. The year-one wellbeing drop is "suggestive". A piece that says the rule "looks worse, then gets better" overclaims on both.
2. Test scores are near zero in the pouch study, so a reader will ask what the payoff of waiting is. The scene must not imply a benefit the paper does not claim.
3. The November national study reports score gains from year one, which contradicts a "wait it out" arc for scores. The two studies use different samples.
4. Brookings reports teen phone use at school rose over 2025-26. A school in year two may be a school where enforcement is slipping, not a school waiting for a payoff.
5. The data is about pouch schools. A school with a different kind of policy does not map onto it.
6. No ban study measures anxiety or depression. Placed next to the Haidt debate, the piece will be read as a verdict on it unless it says otherwise in plain words.
7. One school chosen because it fits is an anecdote, and the piece becomes the original pitch in a better wrapper.

**(b) Has it been done.** For a feature in The Atlantic, The New Yorker, New York magazine, Vox, Wired, NYT Magazine or Slate on a school living through a phone ban, Teodor reported: "I could not find prior coverage", from two or three queries, which he called "a thin negative, not proof the angle is free". Closest pieces he found: Harvard Ed. Magazine, "No Signal" (https://www.gse.harvard.edu/ideas/ed-magazine/24/11/no-signal); EdWeek, "These schools restricted cellphone use. Here's what happened next" (https://www.edweek.org/technology/these-schools-restricted-cellphone-use-heres-what-happened-next/2025/12); Brookings, "A year later" (link above); Maclean's, "Schools vs Screens" (https://macleans.ca/society/schools-vs-screens/, title only). His WebFetch of the Stanford news page returned HTTP 403, so he did not open it.

**Outcome.** He still holds revise, at less than full confidence, and added a fifth condition: do not state the year-three improvement as fact until someone reads the paper's year-by-year results and reports absolute numbers. He would kill if the paper's body shows the year-three wellbeing gain is inside its own noise, or if the named school's data shows no before-and-after change. He would run it with the paper's year-by-year table plus a school that shares its own discipline and survey figures.

## Chair's outside check

**Saturation.** The finding itself is not new. NPR ran "What actually happens when schools take away students' phones?" on 4 May 2026 (https://www.npr.org/2026/05/04/nx-s1-5810191/what-actually-happens-when-schools-take-away-students-phones), and per the search summary the study's own author advises schools to expect more suspensions in the first year. "One year later inside the schools" is also a common news format: Chalkbeat on New York (https://www.chalkbeat.org/newyork/2025/05/23/school-enforced-cell-phone-bans-what-changed/), NPR on Kentucky (https://www.npr.org/2026/02/20/nx-s1-5675979/school-education-kentucky-cell-phone-ban-consequences), the Boston Globe on New Hampshire (https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/08/04/metro/new-hampshire-schools-cellphone-ban-results/), EdSource on California (https://edsource.org/2026/california-school-cellphone-policies/770647?amp=1), KCUR on Missouri (https://www.kcur.org/education/2026-06-22/a-new-set-of-distractions-missouris-ban-on-cellphones-in-schools-still-divides) and the UFT (https://www.uft.org/news/teaching/learning-curve/statewide-cellphone-ban-1-year-later). I read search summaries, not the pages. For a long magazine feature that follows one school through the study's curve, I could not find prior coverage, from one search. So the angle has no new finding and no new format. What it can have that the others lack is one school's own numbers set against the national curve, and that depends entirely on access.

**Register.** The room's shorthand ("worse in year one, better by year three", "a policy that is measurably hurting") is stronger than the paper. The shaped pitch above uses the abstract's words instead. "Measurably hurting" is not supported: the wellbeing drop is "suggestive". I removed it.

**Correction to the room.** The Stanford study is from spring 2026 (NBER issue date April 2026, Stanford News in May), not November. The November news is a different national study. A peg built on "new this month" would be wrong for the pouch study.

**My read.** Revise and resubmit is right, and it is closer to kill than the room's four votes suggest. Without a school, this is a summary of reporting that NPR and Scientific American already published.

## Managing editor findings (separate gate, not in the room)

Verdict: **Revise and resubmit.** "Come back with the school, a principal or teacher on record, and a plan for what the school's own year-one and year-two data will show. Also say the study's school-level average does not tell you what any one school will see. Then this is a green light."

Claims it settled:
- Haidt's book date: 26 March 2024, Penguin Press (https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/729231/the-anxious-generation-by-jonathan-haidt/9780593655030). This replaces Teodor's "from memory, unverified".
- Study design, from the NBER page it opened (https://nber.org/papers/w35132): as set out under "What the evidence says". Thomas Dee is not first in the author order, so do not call him lead author without checking. The paper says "disciplinary incidents"; "suspensions" is a gloss.
- Overall 2011 figure: 28.5% (https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/ss6104a1.htm). It also gave a 2023 figure of 40% from https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/75/su/su7501a4.htm, a page it did not open.
- Iceland: one secondary source says the study covered 70 schools and nearly 24,000 survey responses, was published 27 October 2026 in JAMA Network Open, and concluded bans "may be insufficient to improve adolescent mental health at the population level" (https://www.techlicious.com/blog/school-phone-bans-teen-mental-health-study/). The JAMA page itself was not found.

Novelty: "I could not find prior coverage of that exact angle", from one general query with no archive searches. Adjacent items: the Ford School write-up of the same paper (https://fordschool.umich.edu/news/2026/lockable-phone-pouches-schools-improve-student-well-being-over-time-not-test-scores-or), Chalkbeat Newark (https://www.chalkbeat.org/newark/2026/08/10/school-district-cellphone-ban-pilot-had-positive-results-with-concerns/), Amsterdam News on New York's second year (https://amsterdamnews.com/news/2026/08/03/new-yorks-school-cellphone-policy-enters-its-second-year/) and Global News on Manitoba's second year (https://globalnews.ca/video/11394129/manitoba-schools-entering-second-year-of-cellphone-ban/amp).

## Gaps carried from intake

The pitcher said "just start", so none of these were asked:
- No named sources and no access to any school.
- No specific magazine.
- No news peg. The room did not find one for 2026-11-27. The 17 November national study is the nearest, and it is about test scores.
- No named experts behind "experts say".
- "Rates started rising around 2012", "exactly when smartphones became common" and "rewiring adolescent brains" are the pitcher's assertions with no source. The shaped pitch drops all three.
